claim: Large transcellular pores elicited by bacterial mono-ADP-ribosyltransferase (mART) exotoxins inhibiting the small RhoA GTPase compromise the endothelial barrier.
source: Large transcellular pores elicited by bacterial mono-ADP-ribosyltransferase (mART) exotoxins inhibiting the small RhoA GTPase compromise the endothelial barrier.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that references established knowledge about bacterial toxins and their effects on endothelial barriers.

claim: Membrane tension and bending rigidity are the minimal set of mechanical parameters determining the nucleation and maximal size of transendothelial cell macroaperture (TEM) tunnels induced by bacterial RhoA-targeting mART exotoxins.
source: Recent advances in biophysical modeling point toward membrane tension and bending rigidity as the minimal set of mechanical parameters determining the nucleation and maximal size of transendothelial cell macroaperture (TEM) tunnels induced by bacterial RhoA-targeting mART exotoxins.
evidence: This claim is supported by theoretical modeling described in the manuscript and references to recent advances in biophysical modeling.

claim: Cellular depletion of caveolin-1 increases the number of TEMs per cell.
source: We report that cellular depletion of caveolin-1, the membrane-embedded building block of caveolae, and depletion of cavin-1, the master regulator of caveolae invaginations, increase the number of TEMs per cell.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A showing increased TEM density in siCAV1 conditions.

claim: Cellular depletion of cavin-1 increases the number of TEMs per cell.
source: We report that cellular depletion of caveolin-1, the membrane-embedded building block of caveolae, and depletion of cavin-1, the master regulator of caveolae invaginations, increase the number of TEMs per cell.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A showing increased TEM density in siPTRF conditions.

claim: The enhanced occurrence of TEM nucleation events correlates with a reduction in cell height due to the increase in cell spreading and decrease in cell volume.
source: The enhanced occurrence of TEM nucleation events correlates with a reduction in cell height due to the increase in cell spreading and decrease in cell volume, which, together with the disruption of RhoA-driven F-actin meshwork, favor membrane apposition for TEM nucleation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements of cell area, volume, and calculated height shown in Figure 3 and Table 1.

claim: Caveolin-1 specifically controls the opening speed of TEMs, leading to their dramatic 5.4-fold larger widening.
source: Strikingly, caveolin-1 specifically controls the opening speed of TEMs, leading to their dramatic 5.4-fold larger widening.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B showing maximal TEM areas in different siRNA conditions.

claim: CAV1 KO mice show higher lethality when subjected to a catalytically active mART exotoxin targeting RhoA during staphylococcal bloodstream infection.
source: Consistent with the increase in TEM density and width in siCAV1 cells, we record a higher lethality in CAV1 KO mice subjected to a catalytically active mART exotoxin targeting RhoA during staphylococcal bloodstream infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data shown in Figure 5 comparing Cav1-/- and Cav1+/+ mice infected with S. aureus strains.

claim: Caveolin-1 contributes to membrane stiffening in addition to the role of cavin-1/caveolin-1-dependent caveolae in the control of membrane tension homeostasis.
source: Combined theoretical modeling with independent biophysical measurements of plasma membrane bending rigidity points toward a specific contribution of caveolin-1 to membrane stiffening in addition to the role of cavin-1/caveolin-1-dependent caveolae in the control of membrane tension homeostasis.
evidence: This claim is supported by membrane tether pulling experiments shown in Figure 6D and theoretical modeling described in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The endothelial cell monolayer lining the inner surface of the vascular tree forms an active semipermeable barrier that actively responds to hemodynamic forces to control blood pressure.
source: The endothelial cell monolayer lining the inner surface of the vascular tree forms an active semipermeable barrier that actively responds to hemodynamic forces to control blood pressure (Aird, 2007a; Aird, 2007b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Aird, 2007a and Aird, 2007b.

claim: Regulation of the endothelial barrier involves a bidirectional interplay between actomyosin cytoskeleton and plasma membrane mechanics.
source: Regulation of the endothelial barrier involves a bidirectional interplay between actomyosin cytoskeleton and plasma membrane mechanics, which together control paracellular exchanges at cell–cell junctions (Komarova et al., 2017), as well as transcellular exchanges through less-characterized transcellular openings (Aird, 2007a; Aird, 2007b; Guo et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Komarova et al., 2017, Aird, 2007a, Aird, 2007b, and Guo et al., 2016.

claim: Bacterial mono-ADP-ribosyltransferases (mART) exotoxins catalyze the post-translational modification of the small GTPase RhoA for inhibition.
source: Bacterial mono-ADP-ribosyltransferases (mART) exotoxins, which catalyze the post-translational modification of the small GTPase RhoA for inhibition, induce the spontaneous formation of transendothelial cell macroaperture (TEM) tunnels up to 10–20 µm in diameter (Boyer et al., 2006; Gonzalez-Rodriguez et al., 2020; Maddugoda et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Boyer et al., 2006, Gonzalez-Rodriguez et al., 2020, and Maddugoda et al., 2011.

claim: mART exotoxins induce the spontaneous formation of transendothelial cell macroaperture (TEM) tunnels up to 10–20 µm in diameter.
source: Bacterial mono-ADP-ribosyltransferases (mART) exotoxins, which catalyze the post-translational modification of the small GTPase RhoA for inhibition, induce the spontaneous formation of transendothelial cell macroaperture (TEM) tunnels up to 10–20 µm in diameter (Boyer et al., 2006; Gonzalez-Rodriguez et al., 2020; Maddugoda et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Boyer et al., 2006, Gonzalez-Rodriguez et al., 2020, and Maddugoda et al., 2011.

claim: The mART group includes the exotoxin C3 (ExoC3) from Clostridium botulinum and the epidermal differentiation inhibitors (EDIN) A, B, and C close homologs from Staphylococcus aureus.
source: This group of mART includes the exotoxin C3 (ExoC3) from Clostridium botulinum and the epidermal differentiation inhibitors (EDIN) A, B, and C close homologs from Staphylococcus aureus (Sugai et al., 1992; Chardin et al., 1989; Paterson et al., 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Sugai et al., 1992, Chardin et al., 1989, and Paterson et al., 1990.

claim: The intravenous injection of EDIN or ExoC3 triggers vascular leakage.
source: The intravenous injection of EDIN or ExoC3 triggers vascular leakage (Boyer et al., 2006; Rolando et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Boyer et al., 2006 and Rolando et al., 2009.

claim: EDIN favors the translocation of S. aureus through vascular tissues for dissemination.
source: Cumulative evidence also indicates that EDIN favors the translocation of S. aureus through vascular tissues for dissemination (Munro et al., 2010; Courjon et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Munro et al., 2010 and Courjon et al., 2015.

claim: TEM tunnels form ex vivo in the endothelium lining the inner surface of rat aortas either infected with S. aureus producing the RhoA-targeting EDIN mART or treated with EDIN.
source: Although TEM tunnels have not yet been visualized in vivo, they form ex vivo in the endothelium lining the inner surface of rat aortas either infected with S. aureus producing the RhoA-targeting EDIN mART or treated with EDIN (Boyer et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Boyer et al., 2006.

claim: The inhibition of RhoA signaling by bacterial mART exotoxins disrupts contractile actomyosin stress fibers.
source: Mechanistically, the inhibition of RhoA signaling by bacterial mART exotoxins disrupts contractile actomyosin stress fibers, which otherwise stiffen in response to shear forces exerted by the blood flow that tends to compress cells (Boyer et al., 2006; Gonzalez-Rodriguez et al., 2020; Maddugoda et al., 2011; Sugai et al., 1992; Chardin et al., 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Boyer et al., 2006, Gonzalez-Rodriguez et al., 2020, Maddugoda et al., 2011, Sugai et al., 1992, and Chardin et al., 1989.

claim: Compressive mechanical forces applied to the apical region of endothelial cells bring into close contact the apical and basal plasma membranes to nucleate transcellular pores.
source: In line with this, compressive mechanical forces applied to the apical region of endothelial cells bring into close contact the apical and basal plasma membranes to nucleate transcellular pores (Ng et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ng et al., 2017.

claim: The magnitude of the force required to mechanically open TEMs dramatically decreases when RhoA is inhibited.
source: Although force-induced nucleation of TEMs can be triggered in the absence of inhibition of RhoA, the magnitude of the force required to mechanically open TEMs dramatically decreases when RhoA is inhibited (Ng et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ng et al., 2017.

claim: TEMs form because of a disruption of actomyosin stress fibers under the control of RhoA, which concur to reduce the height of cells as they spread out.
source: This led to postulate that TEMs form because of a disruption of actomyosin stress fibers under the control of RhoA, which concur to reduce the height of cells as they spread out (Boyer et al., 2006; Tsai et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Boyer et al., 2006 and Tsai et al., 2022.

claim: The increase in membrane tension in response to cell spreading is the driving force of TEM nucleation.
source: Notably, the analogy drawn between liquid and cellular dewetting suggests that the increase in membrane tension in response to cell spreading is the driving force of TEM nucleation also contributing to define the initial speed of opening, that is, before that membrane tension relaxation around TEM edges and build-up of an actomyosin bundle encircling TEMs counteract the opening (Maddugoda et al., 2011; Gonzalez-Rodriguez et al., 2012; Stefani et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Maddugoda et al., 2011, Gonzalez-Rodriguez et al., 2012, and Stefani et al., 2017, and represents a theoretical inference from the dewetting model.

claim: Membrane bending rigidity contributes to TEM dynamics due to the high curvature of the plasma membrane at the edge of TEMs.
source: Of note, the high curvature of the plasma membrane at the edge of TEMs also points toward a contribution of membrane bending rigidity, that is, the energy required to locally bend the membrane surface, in their dynamics.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observed high curvature at TEM edges.

claim: Caveolae are mechano-regulators of the plasma membrane that spontaneously flatten to accommodate acute mechanical loads and thereby prevent membrane rupturing.
source: Caveolae are mechano-regulators of the plasma membrane that spontaneously flatten to accommodate acute mechanical loads and thereby prevent membrane rupturing (Sinha et al., 2011; Parton et al., 2020a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Sinha et al., 2011 and Parton et al., 2020a.

claim: Caveolin oligomers are essential components of caveolae pits.
source: Caveolin oligomers are essential components of caveolae pits (Parton et al., 2006; Porta et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Parton et al., 2006 and Porta et al., 2022.

claim: Caveolin-1 homo-oligomers form flat discoid complexes embedded into the inner leaflet of the membrane.
source: Caveolin-1 homo-oligomers form flat discoid complexes embedded into the inner leaflet of the membrane (Porta et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Porta et al., 2022.

claim: The process of invagination of caveolar pits of 50–100 nm diameter involves the association of caveolin-1 with cavin-1 cytosolic structural protein.
source: The process of invagination of caveolar pits of 50–100 nm diameter involves the association of caveolin-1 with cavin-1 cytosolic structural protein (also referred to as PTRF) (Ludwig et al., 2013; Ariotti et al., 2015; Ludwig et al., 2016; Yang and Scarlata, 2017; Lamaze et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ludwig et al., 2013, Ariotti et al., 2015, Ludwig et al., 2016, Yang and Scarlata, 2017, and Lamaze et al., 2017.

claim: Caveolae pits are stabilized at their neck by the assembly of a ring of dynamin-like EHD2 oligomers.
source: Caveolae pits are further stabilized at their neck by the assembly of a ring of dynamin-like EHD2 oligomers (Daumke et al., 2007; Yeow et al., 2017; Nishimura and Suetsugu, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Daumke et al., 2007, Yeow et al., 2017, and Nishimura and Suetsugu, 2022.

claim: In endothelial cells, the crosstalk between caveolin-1 and RhoA during actomyosin contractility leads to critical mechano-sensing and adaptation to hemodynamic forces.
source: In endothelial cells, the crosstalk between caveolin-1 and RhoA during actomyosin contractility leads to critical mechano-sensing and adaptation to hemodynamic forces (Yu et al., 2006; Del Pozo et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Yu et al., 2006 and Del Pozo et al., 2021.

claim: Caveolin-1-deficient mice undergo an increase in the endothelial nitric oxide (eNOS) signaling that is critical to activate RhoA signaling via nitration-mediated inhibition of the GTPase-activating protein (GAP) activity of p190RhoGAP-A.
source: For example, caveolin-1-deficient mice undergo an increase in the endothelial nitric oxide (eNOS) signaling that is critical to activate RhoA signaling via nitration-mediated inhibition of the GTPase-activating protein (GAP) activity of p190RhoGAP-A (Siddiqui et al., 2011; Razani et al., 2001; Miyawaki-Shimizu et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Siddiqui et al., 2011, Razani et al., 2001, and Miyawaki-Shimizu et al., 2006.

claim: ExoC3 treatment reduces the density of invaginated caveolae at the plasma membrane by 1.6-fold.
source: We recorded a 1.6-fold decrease in the mean density of caveolae in the ExoC3-treated cells, which exhibited 3.4 ± 2.1 caveolae/µm2 of membrane, compared to 5.4 ± 3.1 caveolae/µm2 of membrane in untreated cells (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from electron microscopy shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The pool of plasma membrane-located caveolae remaining in ExoC3-treated cells is evenly distributed with no detectable accumulation around TEM tunnels.
source: The pool of plasma membrane-located caveolae remaining in ExoC3-treated cells is evenly distributed with no detectable accumulation around TEM tunnels (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunogold labeling data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: siRNA-mediated depletion of caveolin-1 (siCAV1) strongly reduces both caveolin-1 and the cellular pool of cavin-1/PTRF by approximately 80%.
source: We observed that small interfering RNA (siRNA)-mediated depletion of caveolin-1 (siCAV1) strongly reduces both caveolin-1 and the cellular pool of cavin-1/PTRF by approximately 80% (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: About one-half of the pool of caveolin-1 remained unaffected by the siRNA-targeted depletion of cavin-1/PTRF (siPRTF).
source: In contrast, about one-half of the pool of caveolin-1 remained unaffected by the siRNA-targeted depletion of cavin-1/PTRF (siPRTF) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Both siRNA treatments (siCAV1 and siPTRF) had no effect on the extent of mono-ADPribosylation of RhoA.
source: Both siRNA treatments had no effect on the extent of mono-ADPribosylation of RhoA (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: A higher percentage of cells display at least one TEM in the population of caveolin-1 or cavin-1-deficient cells (37.6 ± 1.3% siCAV1 and 36.4 ± 1.3% siPTRF vs. 28.8 ± 1.2% siCTRL).
source: Quantitative measurements showed a higher percentage of cells displaying at least one TEM in the population of caveolin-1 or cavin-1-deficient cells (37.6 ± 1.3% siCAV1 and 36.4 ± 1.3% siPTRF vs. 28.8 ± 1.2% siCTRL) (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: There is a significant increase in the density of TEMs per cell in siCAV1 (NTEM_siCAV1 = 1.96) and siPTRF (NTEM_siPTRF = 1.36) conditions compared to siCTRL (NsiCTRL = 0.91).
source: Moreover, we observed a significant increase in the density of TEMs per cell in siCAV1 (NTEM_siCAV1 = 1.96) and siPTRF (NTEM_siPTRF = 1.36) conditions compared to siCTRL (NsiCTRL = 0.91) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The efficiency of the formation of TEMs is inversely correlated to the density and stability of caveolae at the plasma membrane.
source: Together, these data show that the efficiency of the formation of TEMs is inversely correlated to the density and stability of caveolae at the plasma membrane.
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing increased TEM formation with caveolae depletion.

claim: ExoC3 treatment induces a significant increase in actin mesh size of about 0.2 μm2 compared to non-intoxicated cells.
source: In all conditions of siRNA treatment, we have measured that ExoC3 treatment induces a significant increase in actin mesh size of about 0.2 μm2 compared to non-intoxicated cells (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by 2D STORM imaging data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: No significant difference of mesh size was recorded between siCTRL, siCAV1, or siPTRF conditions before and after treatment with ExoC3.
source: No significant difference of mesh size was recorded between siCTRL, siCAV1, or siPTRF conditions before and after treatment with ExoC3 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by 2D STORM imaging data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: RhoA inhibition generates a loose F-actin meshwork framing large cellular zones devoid of F-actin of same extent in all siRNA conditions.
source: We concluded that in addition to the well-established impact of RhoA inhibition on actin stress fibers it generates a loose F-actin meshwork framing large cellular zones devoid of F-actin of same extent in all siRNA conditions.
evidence: This claim is based on 2D STORM imaging observations shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Upon intoxication of siCTRL-treated cells, there is a significant increase of 36% of the spreading area together with 17% increase of the cell volume.
source: Upon intoxication of siCTRL-treated cells, we recorded a significant increase of 36% of the spreading area together with 17% increase of the cell volume (Figure 3C and D and Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 3C and D and Table 1.

claim: The dominant impact of cell area changes over the volume parameter accounts for the calculated decrease of cell height of 15% in siCTRL-treated cells upon ExoC3 intoxication.
source: The dominant impact of cell area changes over the volume parameter accounts for the calculated decrease of cell height of 15% (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is based on calculations from measured cell area and volume data shown in Table 1.

claim: When siCAV1- and siPTRF-transfected cells were treated with ExoC3, there is a reduction in cell volume concomitant to the increase in their spreading area.
source: Hence, when siCAV1- and siPTRF-transfected cells were treated with ExoC3, we recorded a reduction in cell volume concomitant to the increase in their spreading area (Figure 3C and D and Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 3C and D and Table 1.

claim: The reinforced reduction in cell height recorded in siCAV1 or siPTRF-treated cells is in good agreement with findings showing that these treatments increase the density of TEMs.
source: The reinforced reduction in cell height recorded in siCAV1 or siPTRF-treated cells is in good agreement with our findings showing that these treatments increase the density of TEMs.
evidence: This claim is an inference connecting cell height measurements with TEM density observations.

claim: In the absence of ExoC3, the effects of siPTRF on cell shape parameters were slightly stronger than those of siCAV1.
source: Note that in the absence of ExoC3 we recorded that the effects of siPTRF on cell shape parameters were slightly stronger than those of siCAV1, thereby highlighting the key involvement of caveolae in the control of cell height (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: The depletion of caveolae and the inhibition of RhoA work together to reduce cell height that favors together with the loss of F-actin the nucleation of TEMs.
source: The depletion of caveolae and the inhibition of RhoA work together to reduce cell height that favors together with the loss of F-actin the nucleation of TEMs.
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the combined effects of caveolae depletion and RhoA inhibition on cell height and TEM formation.

claim: TEMs are 5.4-fold wider in siCAV1-treated cells compared to siPTRF- and siCTRL-treatments.
source: Interestingly, we recorded 5.4-fold wider TEMs in siCAV1-treated cells compared to siPTRF- and siCTRL-treatments (Figure 4B and Videos 1–3).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurements of maximal TEM areas shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The time for TEMs to reach their maximal diameter (tmax) and the overall TEM cycles (tc) remains identical in all conditions.
source: Interestingly, the time for TEMs to reach their maximal diameter (tmax) and the overall TEM cycles (tc) remains identical in all conditions (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: There is a twofold higher opening speed in caveolin-1-depleted cells: So_siCAV1 = 2.4 µm2/s versus So_siCTRL = 1.1 µm2/s in control cells.
source: Strikingly, we recorded a twofold higher opening speed in caveolin-1-depleted cells: So_siCAV1 = 2.4 µm2/s versus So_siCTRL = 1.1 µm2/s in control cells, which contrasts with the minor impact of siPTRF with So_siPTRF = 1.7 µm2/s (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by high temporal resolution imaging data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Caveolin-1 has a specific function in the regulation of the opening speed of TEMs that has a critical impact on TEM maximal width.
source: In conclusion, we have identified a specific function of caveolin-1 in the regulation of the opening speed of TEMs that has a critical impact on TEM maximal width.
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the experimental data on TEM opening speeds and maximal widths.

claim: The loss of caveolin-1 expression sensitizes mice to bloodstream infection triggered by S. aureus-produced EDIN-B.
source: The loss of caveolin-1 expression thus sensitizes mice to bloodstream infection triggered by S. aureus-produced EDIN-B.
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the survival data comparing Cav1-/- and Cav1+/+ mice.

claim: When Cav1-/- mice were challenged with LD50 of S. aureus (2.5 × 10^7 CFU/m), there was lower survival with S. aureus WT edinB (n = 11 death/18 mice) compared to ΔedinB (n = 4 death/17 mice).
source: When we challenged Cav1-/- mice with this LD50 of S. aureus (2.5 × 107 CFU/m), we saw a lower survival with S. aureus WT edinB (n = 11 death/18 mice) compared to ΔedinB (n = 4 death/17 mice) (p=0.0123, Mantel‒Cox test) (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: There is a significant decrease in survival in caveolin-1-deficient mice infected with ΔedinB pEDIN-B compared to mice infected with ΔedinB pEDIN-B-RE.
source: We saw a significant decrease in survival in caveolin-1-deficient mice infected with ΔedinB pEDIN-B compared to mice infected with ΔedinB pEDIN-B-RE.
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data comparing mice infected with catalytically active versus inactive EDIN-B.

claim: In the context of bloodstream infection by S. aureus, caveolin-1 expression confers a resistance to the pathogenicity triggered by EDIN-B mART activity on RhoA.
source: We concluded that in the context of bloodstream infection by S. aureus, caveolin-1 expression confers a resistance to the pathogenicity triggered by EDIN-B mART activity on RhoA.
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the survival experiments comparing wildtype and catalytically inactive EDIN-B.

claim: Cells treated with siCAV1 have a significant twofold higher membrane tension than the controls.
source: From our measurements, we deduce that cells treated with siCAV1 have a significant twofold higher membrane tension than the controls, and no effect in siPTRF-treated cells (see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This claim is based on theoretical modeling and experimental measurements described in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The model predicts a 55% reduction in membrane rigidity from a loss of expression of caveolin-1 and a lower reduction of 15% upon a loss of cavin-1 expression.
source: Using the following values for the siCTRL-treated cells – an initial membrane tension σ0 = 2.5 10–5 N/m (Raucher and Sheetz, 2000) and a bending rigidity κsiCTRL = 23.4 kBT (direct measurement, see below) – the model predicts a 55% reduction in membrane rigidity from a loss of expression of caveolin-1 and a lower reduction of 15% upon a loss of cavin-1 expression.
evidence: This claim is based on theoretical modeling using measured parameters and cited values from Raucher and Sheetz, 2000.

claim: There is a significant decrease of 30% of the bending rigidity from κsiCTRL = 23.4 ± 0.9 kBT to κsiCAV1 = 17.0 ± 0.9 kBT.
source: We measured a significant decrease of 30% of the bending rigidity from κsiCTRL = 23.4 ± 0.9 kBT to κsiCAV1 = 17.0 ± 0.9 kBT.
evidence: This claim is supported by membrane tether pulling experiments shown in Figure 6D.

claim: There is no significant difference in bending rigidity in siPTRF conditions compared to siCTRL, with a κsiPTRF = 23.4 ± 1.3 kBT.
source: Moreover, we observed no significant difference in siPTRF conditions compared to siCTRL, with a κsiPTRF = 23.4 ± 1.3 kBT (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by membrane tether pulling experiments shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The expression of caveolin-1, but not of cavin-1, significantly stiffens the plasma membrane.
source: In good agreement with the theoretical predictions, these measurements establish that the expression of caveolin-1, but not of cavin-1, significantly stiffens the plasma membrane.
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the membrane tether pulling experiments and theoretical modeling.

claim: siRNA-mediated knockdown of key structural and regulatory components of caveolae sensitizes endothelial cells to the formation of TEM tunnels triggered by the inhibition of RhoA-driven actomyosin contractility.
source: We report that siRNA-mediated knockdown of key structural and regulatory components of caveolae sensitizes endothelial cells to the formation of TEM tunnels triggered by the inhibition of RhoA-driven actomyosin contractility.
evidence: This claim summarizes the main findings from the TEM formation experiments.

claim: Inhibition of RhoA reduces by twofold the pool of caveolae invaginations at the plasma membrane.
source: Hence, inhibition of RhoA reduces by twofold the pool of caveolae invaginations at the plasma membrane.
evidence: This claim is supported by electron microscopy data showing reduced caveolae density in ExoC3-treated cells.

claim: Targeted depletion of caveolin-1 and cavin-1 caveolae decreases cell volume and increases cell spreading, which concur to decrease the height of cells favoring membrane apposition for TEM nucleation.
source: Mechanistically, we report that targeted depletion of caveolin-1 and cavin-1 caveolae decreases cell volume and increases cell spreading, which concur to decrease the height of cells favoring membrane apposition for TEM nucleation.
evidence: This claim is supported by cell volume and spreading area measurements shown in Figure 3 and Table 1.

claim: There is a higher susceptibility of Cav1-deficient mice to lethal effects triggered by EDIN-B mART during staphylococcal bloodstream infection.
source: In good agreement with the recorded increase in TEM formation and width following caveolin-1 knockdown, we establish a higher susceptibility of Cav1-deficient mice to lethal effects triggered by EDIN-B mART during staphylococcal bloodstream infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data from mouse infection experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: In addition to the well-established role of caveolae in membrane tension homeostasis, caveolin-1 rigidifies plasma membrane either directly or indirectly.
source: Finally, we provide theoretical and experimental evidence that in addition to the well-established role of caveolae in membrane tension homeostasis, caveolin-1 rigidifies plasma membrane either directly or indirectly, as discussed below.
evidence: This claim is supported by membrane tether pulling experiments and theoretical modeling.

claim: Caveolin-1 depletion decreases membrane bending rigidity by 30%.
source: Our biophysical measurements unravel that caveolin-1 depletion decreases membrane bending rigidity by 30%, while depletion of cavin-1 has no impact.
evidence: This claim is supported by membrane tether pulling experiments shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Depletion of cavin-1 has no impact on membrane bending rigidity.
source: Our biophysical measurements unravel that caveolin-1 depletion decreases membrane bending rigidity by 30%, while depletion of cavin-1 has no impact.
evidence: This claim is supported by membrane tether pulling experiments shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The difference between the 30% experimental decrease and 55% theoretical decrease in bending rigidity can be attributed to several approximations in the theoretical model.
source: The difference recorded between these approaches can be attributed to several approximations in the theoretical model, notably the simplified treatment of the physical membrane tension variation, the cytoskeletal contributions, and the interactions between neighboring TEM tunnels.
evidence: This claim is an inference discussing the limitations of the theoretical model.

claim: Caveolin-1 is inserted in the cytosolic leaflet of the plasma membrane.
source: Indeed, since caveolin-1 is inserted in the cytosolic leaflet of the plasma membrane, when a nanotube is pulled toward the exterior of the PMS, we can expect two situations depending on the ability of caveolin-1 to deform membranes, which remains to be addressed (Porta et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Porta et al., 2022 and represents established knowledge about caveolin-1 membrane topology.

claim: A very reduced concentration of Cav1 compared to the plasma membrane has been reported in tunneling nanotubes (TNT) connecting two neighboring cells.
source: Note that the presence of a very reduced concentration of Cav1 compared to the plasma membrane has been reported in tunneling nanotubes (TNT) connecting two neighboring cells (Li et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Li et al., 2022.

claim: Previous studies showed that inclusion of integral proteins in membranes had no impact on bending rigidity, as shown in the bacteriorhodopsin experiment.
source: Considering a direct mechanical role of Cav1, previous studies showed that inclusion of integral proteins in membranes had no impact on bending rigidity, as shown in the bacteriorhodopsin experiment (Manneville et al., 1999), or even decreased membrane rigidity as reported for the Ca2+-ATPase SERCA (Girard et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Manneville et al., 1999 and Girard et al., 2005.

claim: Previous simulations have confirmed the softening effect of protein inclusions.
source: Previous simulations have also confirmed the softening effect of protein inclusions (Fowler et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Fowler et al., 2016.

claim: Caveolae are enriched with cholesterol, sphingomyelin, and glycosphingolipids, including gangliosides.
source: Considering an impact on lipid composition, it is well established that caveolae are enriched with cholesterol, sphingomyelin, and glycosphingolipids, including gangliosides (Parton et al., 2020b; Roitenberg et al., 2018), which are known to rigidify membranes (Rawicz et al., 2008; Steinkühler et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Parton et al., 2020b and Roitenberg et al., 2018.

claim: Cholesterol, sphingomyelin, and glycosphingolipids are known to rigidify membranes.
source: Considering an impact on lipid composition, it is well established that caveolae are enriched with cholesterol, sphingomyelin, and glycosphingolipids, including gangliosides (Parton et al., 2020b; Roitenberg et al., 2018), which are known to rigidify membranes (Rawicz et al., 2008; Steinkühler et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Rawicz et al., 2008 and Steinkühler et al., 2019.

claim: Caveolin-1 might contribute to the enrichment of the plasma membrane with cholesterol, sphingomyelin, and glycosphingolipids.
source: Thus, caveolin-1 might contribute to the enrichment of the plasma membrane with these lipid species.
evidence: This claim is speculation based on the known lipid composition of caveolae and the observed effects of caveolin-1 on membrane rigidity.

claim: The Young's modulus of the cell cortex dramatically decreases in ExoC3-treated cells.
source: Nevertheless, it has been reported that the Young's modulus of the cell cortex dramatically decreases in ExoC3-treated cells (Ng et al., 2017), suggesting a small additional contribution of caveolin-1 depletion to membrane softening.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ng et al., 2017.

claim: 2D STORM data show a dramatic reorganization of actin cytoskeleton in ExoC3-treated cells into a loose F-actin meshwork that is not significantly exacerbated by caveolin-1 depletion.
source: This is supported by 2D STORM data showing a dramatic reorganization of actin cytoskeleton in ExoC3-treated cells into a loose F-actin meshwork that is not significantly exacerbated by caveolin-1 depletion.
evidence: This claim is supported by 2D STORM imaging data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The presence of Cav1 stiffens plasma membranes.
source: Altogether, our results suggest that the presence of Cav1 stiffens plasma membranes, and that the exact origin of this effect must be further investigated.
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the experimental results on membrane bending rigidity.

claim: Membrane rigidity sets the maximal size of TEM aperture.
source: Our study shows that membrane rigidity sets the maximal size of TEM aperture, although an actin ring appears before TEM closure (Stefani et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data on TEM sizes and citation to Stefani et al., 2017.

claim: Cavin-1-dependent caveolae have a function in the regulation of cell height.
source: Our data establish a function to cavin-1-dependent caveolae in the regulation of cell height.
evidence: This claim is supported by cell height measurements shown in Figure 3 and Table 1.

claim: Cell homeostasis during spreading is achieved by decreasing cell volume.
source: This is consistent with findings showing that cell homeostasis during spreading is achieved by decreasing cell volume.
evidence: This claim references established knowledge about cell volume regulation during spreading.

claim: The coupling between variations in cell spreading area and cell volume is breached by disrupting cortical contractility, resulting in cell swelling.
source: Such a coupling between variations in cell spreading area and cell volume is breached by disrupting cortical contractility, resulting in cell swelling (Xie et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Xie et al., 2018.

claim: The ExoC3-triggered increase in endothelial cell spreading occurs concomitantly with a decrease in cell volume.
source: Consistently, we show that the ExoC3-triggered increase in endothelial cell spreading occurs concomitantly with a decrease in cell volume.
evidence: This claim is supported by cell volume and spreading measurements shown in Figure 3.

claim: The decrease in cell volume upon depletion of cavin-1, and to a lesser extent after depletion of caveolin-1, occurs independently of RhoA signaling.
source: Here, we show that the decrease in cell volume upon depletion of cavin-1, and to a lesser extent after depletion of caveolin-1, occurs independently of RhoA signaling, that is, in ExoC3-treated cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by cell volume measurements in ExoC3-treated cells with different siRNA treatments shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Depletion of caveolae and RhoA inactivation may release membrane-folding-driven mechanical constraints that would limit cell spreading.
source: Our findings also suggest that depletion of caveolae and RhoA inactivation may release membrane-folding-driven mechanical constraints that would limit cell spreading.
evidence: This claim is speculation based on the observed effects of caveolae depletion and RhoA inhibition on cell spreading.

claim: Nucleation of TEMs requires the apposition of the basal and apical cell membranes, which is hindered by the intermembrane distance, set by the cell height.
source: Nucleation of TEMs requires the apposition of the basal and apical cell membranes, which is hindered by the intermembrane distance, set by the cell height.
evidence: This claim is based on the physical understanding of TEM nucleation and the role of cell height.

claim: The size of the minimal precursor tunnel required to give rise to a TEM increases with membrane bending rigidity and decreases with membrane tension.
source: The size of the minimal precursor tunnel required to give rise to a TEM increases with membrane bending rigidity and decreases with membrane tension (Gonzalez-Rodriguez et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Gonzalez-Rodriguez et al., 2012 and represents a theoretical prediction.

claim: Silencing cavin-1 leads to a decrease in cell height, thus favoring the likelihood of precursor tunnel nucleation.
source: Silencing cavin-1 or caveolin-1 both lead to a decrease in cell height, thus favoring the likelihood of precursor tunnel nucleation.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on cell height measurements and the understanding of TEM nucleation requirements.

claim: Silencing caveolin-1 leads to a decrease in cell height, thus favoring the likelihood of precursor tunnel nucleation.
source: Silencing cavin-1 or caveolin-1 both lead to a decrease in cell height, thus favoring the likelihood of precursor tunnel nucleation.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on cell height measurements and the understanding of TEM nucleation requirements.

claim: Silencing cavin-1 has no significant impact on either membrane tension or bending rigidity.
source: While silencing cavin-1 has no significant impact on either membrane tension or bending rigidity, silencing caveolin results in both an increase in membrane tension and a decrease in bending rigidity, which results in a decrease in the required minimal radius of the precursor tunnel, thus further favoring TEM nucleation.
evidence: This claim is supported by membrane tension and bending rigidity measurements.

claim: Silencing caveolin-1 results in both an increase in membrane tension and a decrease in bending rigidity.
source: While silencing cavin-1 has no significant impact on either membrane tension or bending rigidity, silencing caveolin results in both an increase in membrane tension and a decrease in bending rigidity, which results in a decrease in the required minimal radius of the precursor tunnel, thus further favoring TEM nucleation.
evidence: This claim is supported by membrane tension and bending rigidity measurements.

claim: A human genetics study pinpointed the impact of haploinsufficiency of the OTULIN deubiquitinase in sensitizing host cells to lysis triggered by the highly prevalent α-hemolysin pore-forming toxin of S. aureus.
source: Indeed, a human genetics study pinpointed the impact of haploinsufficiency of the OTULIN deubiquitinase in sensitizing host cells to lysis triggered by the highly prevalent α-hemolysin pore-forming toxin of S. aureus, a major determinant in staphylococcal pneumonia (Spaan et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Spaan et al., 2022.

claim: The defect in OTULIN activity led to an increase in caveolin-1 cellular protein levels in dermal cells, which in turn upregulates the expression of the ADAM10 receptor of α-hemolysin pore-forming toxin.
source: The defect in OTULIN activity led to an increase in caveolin-1 cellular protein levels in dermal cells, which in turn upregulates the expression of the ADAM10 receptor of α-hemolysin pore-forming toxin.
evidence: This claim references findings from the Spaan et al., 2022 study.

claim: Caveolin-1 expression is not regulated by RhoA signaling.
source: Here, we report that caveolin-1 expression is not regulated by RhoA signaling.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The loss of caveolin-1 expression sensitizes mice to the lethal effects triggered by EDIN-B mART activity on RhoA during S. aureus septicemia.
source: Furthermore, we establish that the loss of caveolin-1 expression sensitizes mice to the lethal effects triggered by EDIN-B mART activity on RhoA during S. aureus septicemia, thus ascribing a pathogenicity potential to this exotoxin that is counteracted by the expression of caveolin-1.
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data from mouse infection experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: A recent analysis of an observational cohort of patients with S. aureus community-acquired pneumonia indicated that EDIN-B, together with Panton–Valentin leukocidin, are positively associated with the etiology of hemoptysis.
source: In line with this, a recent analysis of an observational cohort of patients with S. aureus community-acquired pneumonia indicated that EDIN-B, together with Panton–Valentin leukocidin, are positively associated with the etiology of hemoptysis, manifested by the presence of blood in sputum (Gillet et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Gillet et al., 2021.

claim: RhoA inhibition reduces paracellular permeability while dramatically increasing transcellular permeability.
source: Such a hypothesis is supported by previous findings showing that RhoA inhibition reduces paracellular permeability while dramatically increasing transcellular permeability, and that ADP-ribosyltransferases targeting RhoA increase vascular permeability to the point of animal death when TEM enlargement is no longer controlled (Boyer et al., 2006; Rolando et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Boyer et al., 2006 and Rolando et al., 2009.

claim: ADP-ribosyltransferases targeting RhoA increase vascular permeability to the point of animal death when TEM enlargement is no longer controlled.
source: Such a hypothesis is supported by previous findings showing that RhoA inhibition reduces paracellular permeability while dramatically increasing transcellular permeability, and that ADP-ribosyltransferases targeting RhoA increase vascular permeability to the point of animal death when TEM enlargement is no longer controlled (Boyer et al., 2006; Rolando et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Boyer et al., 2006 and Rolando et al., 2009.

claim: Variations in caveolin-1 expression have a bidirectional impact on host susceptibility to S. aureus infection.
source: Collectively, these findings ascribe to variations in caveolin-1 expression a bidirectional impact on host susceptibility to S. aureus infection, pointing to a possible role of TEM tunnels.
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the combined findings on caveolin-1's role in both α-hemolysin susceptibility and EDIN-B pathogenicity.
